topics.title: What System Design Means
topics.description: Understand system design as the disciplined process of turning product requirements into a reliable, scalable architecture.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Define requirements, constraints, scale, APIs, data flows, bottlenecks, and failure behavior before choosing technologies.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
System design connects user behavior, workload, data, infrastructure, and operational constraints. Begin with what the system must accomplish, then identify quality targets such as latency, availability, durability, security, and growth. A useful design is not the one with the most components; it is the smallest architecture that can satisfy the stated requirements while leaving a practical path for growth. Think in flows: a request enters through an edge layer, reaches application logic, accesses data or cache, and may trigger asynchronous work.

Deeper reasoning:
A useful way to reason about a design is to trace one representative request from the client to the final state change, then identify every dependency on that path. Repeat the exercise for background work and failure recovery. This exposes unnecessary hops and makes the architecture explainable.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Design a course platform where users read lessons, submit quizzes, and receive progress updates. The synchronous request can authenticate the learner, read the lesson, and record a quiz result. Thumbnail generation, analytics events, recommendation updates, and email notifications can happen later. This separation keeps the page responsive without losing secondary work.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Start every design by writing functional requirements and measurable non-functional targets. Estimate traffic and data size before selecting infrastructure. For each major component, identify its dependency, bottleneck, failure behavior, and scaling strategy. This requirement-first approach prevents unnecessary technology choices.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Trace one request end to end, then trace an asynchronous path and a failure-recovery path. The resulting dependency graph is the mental model.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Ask: what are the functional requirements, traffic shape, latency/availability targets, data size, consistency needs, and failure assumptions?

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid treating what system design means as a universal solution. State assumptions, identify the main bottleneck or failure mode, and explain the operational cost. Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
Do not start with Kafka, Redis, or Kubernetes. Start with requirements and derive components.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
An interview-quality design explains why each component exists and what trade-off it introduces.

In production, pair the design with monitoring, capacity limits, safe rollout and a recovery procedure. Define what operators should observe when the component is degraded.

topics.title: Modularization
topics.description: Learn how to divide a large application into components with coherent responsibilities and controlled dependencies.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Partition around business capabilities and ownership, keeping contracts explicit and dependencies intentional.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Modularization groups related behavior behind clear boundaries. A module should own a meaningful business capability rather than merely a few classes. Good boundaries reduce the amount of knowledge one component needs about another. They also make scaling more selective: a search workload can grow independently of order processing. However, every boundary adds communication, deployment, monitoring, and failure overhead, so fragmentation is not automatically an improvement.

Deeper reasoning:
Boundaries should follow ownership and change. If two components always need the same transaction and constantly call each other, separating them may create distributed complexity without real independence. A strong boundary reduces both conceptual coupling and operational coupling.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Consider an online learning product with Identity, Course, Enrollment, Payment, Search, and Notification modules. The Enrollment module can expose an operation such as enroll(userId, courseId) without exposing its database tables. If Search later moves to a specialized index, the rest of the application continues using the same search contract.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Choose boundaries around ownership and change patterns. Keep interfaces explicit, avoid shared mutable internals, and define who owns each piece of data. Measure the cost of remote calls before splitting a tightly coupled workflow into many networked services.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of modules as boxes with contracts. A box should expose behavior, not its internal tables or implementation details.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Ask whether a proposed boundary creates fewer dependencies than it removes; distributed boundaries add latency and failure modes.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid treating modularization as a universal solution. State assumptions, identify the main bottleneck or failure mode, and explain the operational cost. Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
Prefer a modular monolith when independent deployment is not yet valuable; split services when ownership and scaling justify it.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
A module boundary is useful when it reduces coupling or lets a capability change, scale, or deploy independently.

In production, pair the design with monitoring, capacity limits, safe rollout and a recovery procedure. Define what operators should observe when the component is degraded.

topics.title: Abstraction
topics.description: Understand how stable interfaces hide implementation details and reduce coupling.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Hide implementation details behind stable contracts while exposing important semantics such as consistency and errors.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Abstraction exposes what a component promises rather than how it performs the work. A client should depend on a stable contract such as createOrder or getUserProfile, while storage engines, caches, retries, and internal workers remain behind that contract. This lets implementations evolve without forcing every caller to change. Good abstraction also reduces cognitive load because each component can reason about a smaller surface area.

Deeper reasoning:
An abstraction is valuable only when its contract captures the behavior callers actually depend on. If callers must understand storage quirks, retry rules, or provider-specific errors to use the abstraction correctly, the boundary is leaking implementation details.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A document service can expose storeDocument(ownerId, content). Internally it may place large content in object storage, store metadata in a database, calculate a checksum, and emit a processing event. A caller only needs the result and the contract; it does not need to coordinate those internal steps.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Keep abstractions honest. Do not hide important semantics such as eventual consistency, retry behavior, or partial failure. A small interface with clear guarantees is more useful than a generic interface that conceals too many special cases.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The best abstraction preserves the guarantees callers need while allowing the implementation behind it to evolve.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interviewers often ask when an abstraction becomes harmful: answer when callers must understand hidden provider/storage quirks.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid treating abstraction as a universal solution. State assumptions, identify the main bottleneck or failure mode, and explain the operational cost. Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
Use interfaces at genuine change boundaries, not simply because every class needs an interface.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
Good abstractions reduce coupling; leaky abstractions merely rename implementation details.

topics.title: Layering
topics.description: Learn how presentation, application, business, data-access, and storage responsibilities can be separated.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Separate concerns such as edge handling, application orchestration, domain rules, persistence, and infrastructure.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Layering separates concerns by responsibility. A presentation layer handles interaction, an application layer coordinates use cases, business logic enforces domain rules, a data-access layer translates persistence operations, and storage provides durable state. The exact number of layers can vary, but the principle is to prevent unrelated concerns from leaking into one another. This improves testing because each layer can be exercised with controlled dependencies.

Deeper reasoning:
Layering is especially useful when responsibilities have different reasons to change. User-interface changes should not require database changes, and storage changes should not rewrite domain rules. The layers should communicate through explicit contracts rather than shared assumptions.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: For a learning portal, a browser calls an API endpoint. The application layer validates the command and invokes EnrollmentService. That service applies enrollment rules and uses EnrollmentRepository to persist the result. The repository hides SQL details from the business logic, allowing the storage implementation to change without rewriting the enrollment rules.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Avoid both extremes: direct database access from every layer and excessive layers that add no value. Keep dependency direction deliberate, define DTOs or contracts at boundaries, and test business rules without requiring a live database when possible.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Each layer should answer one kind of question. Domain rules should not depend on HTTP headers or SQL syntax.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain why direct controller-to-database code becomes difficult to validate, secure, and evolve.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid treating layering as a universal solution. State assumptions, identify the main bottleneck or failure mode, and explain the operational cost. Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
Use enough layers to separate different reasons to change; avoid ceremonial layers with no responsibility.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
Layering controls dependency direction and makes business logic easier to test independently.

topics.title: Scalability
topics.description: Understand horizontal and vertical scaling and the state-management issues that appear when adding nodes.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Scale the bottleneck through vertical or horizontal capacity, while controlling shared state and contention.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Vertical scaling increases the resources of one machine, while horizontal scaling adds more machines or instances. Horizontal scaling is attractive when requests can be distributed and application nodes can operate independently. Stateful sessions make this harder because a request sent to a different node may not see local state. Shared state stores, signed tokens, or carefully controlled affinity can solve different versions of that problem.

Deeper reasoning:
Scaling is ultimately about removing a limiting resource. If CPU is saturated, more application instances may help; if the database is saturated, adding application instances can make the problem worse. Always connect the scaling action to the measured bottleneck.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Suppose a quiz API receives 2,000 requests per second. Instead of placing all traffic on one large server, run several stateless API instances behind a load balancer. Authentication state can live in a shared store or be represented by a verifiable token, while files are kept outside the application instances.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Scale the actual bottleneck, not every component. Horizontal scaling requires attention to connection pools, shared state, data contention, deployment safety, and uneven traffic. A larger machine can be simpler when the workload still fits comfortably on one node.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Scaling is resource conservation: find what saturates first, then increase that resource or reduce demand.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss throughput, concurrency, connection pools, database capacity, hot keys, and uneven workloads—not just server count.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid treating scalability as a universal solution. State assumptions, identify the main bottleneck or failure mode, and explain the operational cost. Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
Scale horizontally when workload and architecture benefit; vertical scaling can be simpler and perfectly valid at moderate scale.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
Horizontal scaling works best when application instances are stateless and shared state is externalized appropriately.

topics.title: Performance
topics.description: Learn to reason about latency, throughput, resource utilization, and bottlenecks.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Treat latency as an end-to-end budget and optimize measured bottlenecks.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Latency measures how long an operation takes; throughput measures how much work completes per unit time. Performance depends on the entire critical path, including network hops, serialization, database queries, locks, CPU, memory, disk, and connection pools. Optimizing a small component has little value when another dependency dominates the request. Measure first, identify the bottleneck, then change the limiting resource.

Deeper reasoning:
Performance should be reasoned about as a budget. If the end-to-end target is 300 ms, decide how much of that budget can be consumed by network calls, application work, storage, and serialization. This makes optimization concrete and prevents spending effort on insignificant portions of the path.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: An API averages 40 ms of application processing but waits 350 ms for a database query. Reducing JSON serialization from 5 ms to 2 ms barely changes end-to-end latency. Adding the right index or changing the query plan could remove most of the delay because the database is the dominant portion of the critical path.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Track p50, p95, and p99 latency rather than only averages. Watch throughput, saturation, queue depth, database latency, cache hit rate, and error rate together. Performance improvements should be validated under realistic concurrency and data volume.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Performance is the sum of the critical path plus queueing. Under load, utilization can increase latency nonlinearly.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain why optimizing a 2 ms operation is irrelevant when a dependency consumes 300 ms.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid treating performance as a universal solution. State assumptions, identify the main bottleneck or failure mode, and explain the operational cost. Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
Profile before optimizing; use caching, batching, indexing, connection pooling, async work, or fewer hops when evidence supports them.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
Use p50, p95, and p99 latency with throughput and saturation metrics; averages can hide tail latency.

topics.title: Security
topics.description: Learn how confidentiality, integrity, availability, authentication, authorization, and layered controls shape architecture.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability across every trust boundary.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Security is a system property rather than a single login feature. Confidentiality protects information from unauthorized disclosure, integrity protects it from unauthorized modification, and availability protects access for legitimate users. Architecture should combine transport protection, authentication, authorization, input validation, secret management, rate limiting, network boundaries, logging, and appropriate encryption. Each layer should assume another control might fail.

Deeper reasoning:
Security decisions should follow data and trust boundaries. Identify what enters the system from an untrusted client, where identity is established, where authorization is checked, and where sensitive data is stored or transmitted. Then make each boundary enforce the smallest required privilege.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A user can successfully sign in to an accounting application, but that does not grant access to every invoice. Authentication establishes the identity; authorization checks whether that identity can access a particular invoice. The API can enforce ownership checks before returning the document and can record security-relevant actions for later investigation.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Apply least privilege, validate untrusted input at boundaries, avoid embedding secrets in source code, and limit public endpoints. Security controls should be designed into data flows, not added only after the functional architecture is complete.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Map data and trust boundaries first. Every transition from untrusted input to privileged action needs explicit controls.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interviewers often probe broken authorization, secret exposure, replay, injection, and excessive privileges.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid treating security as a universal solution. State assumptions, identify the main bottleneck or failure mode, and explain the operational cost. Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
Use defense in depth and least privilege; never rely on a gateway alone for object-level authorization.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
Authentication answers who the caller is; authorization answers what that identity may do. Encryption, validation, secrets, rate limits, and auditability complement those controls.

topics.title: Fault Tolerance and Resilience
topics.description: Understand how systems continue useful work when servers, networks, dependencies, or deployments fail.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Design for component failure with timeouts, bounded retries, isolation, redundancy, graceful degradation, and recovery.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Fault tolerance means the system can continue operating despite selected component failures. Resilience is the broader ability to absorb faults, recover, and return to normal behavior. Common techniques include timeouts, bounded retries, exponential backoff with jitter, circuit breakers, replication, queues, fallbacks, and graceful degradation. The correct combination depends on whether the operation is critical, retryable, idempotent, and latency-sensitive.

Deeper reasoning:
Resilience is about behavior under stress, not only normal operation. Define whether a dependency failure should block, retry, queue, degrade, or fail fast. Different operations can legitimately choose different behavior even inside the same application.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: If a recommendation provider becomes unavailable, a shopping application can temporarily show popular products instead of blocking checkout. A timeout prevents an indefinitely waiting request; a circuit breaker stops repeated calls to a failing dependency; a queue can preserve work that does not need immediate completion.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Never add retries without considering amplification. If 1,000 callers each retry a failing dependency several times, the outage can become worse. Bound retry counts, add jitter, distinguish transient from permanent failures, and make repeated operations safe where possible.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Every dependency needs a defined failure policy: wait, retry, fail, queue, fallback, or shed load.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain how timeout, circuit breaker, bulkhead, fallback, and idempotency solve different parts of failure handling.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid treating fault tolerance and resilience as a universal solution. State assumptions, identify the main bottleneck or failure mode, and explain the operational cost. Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
Use graceful degradation for non-critical dependencies and fail closed or fail safe where correctness or security requires it.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
Resilience is not merely adding retries; retries can amplify an outage.

topics.title: DNS
topics.description: Understand name resolution, caching, TTL, and how DNS participates in service routing.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Use DNS as a cached naming and routing layer whose TTL and resolver behavior affect operational changes.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
DNS translates human-readable names into network destinations. A recursive resolver may answer from cache or follow the hierarchy toward authoritative servers. Caching reduces lookup work, while TTL controls how long a result may remain cached. DNS is therefore both a naming mechanism and an operational consideration: changing an address does not mean every client immediately forgets the previous answer.

Deeper reasoning:
DNS is cached at several layers, so operational changes must account for stale answers. Treat DNS records as part of the deployment plan, and make sure the application remains safe during the period when old and new destinations can both receive traffic.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A learning website uses api.example.test for its API. A client asks a recursive resolver for the address. If the resolver has a valid cached answer, it can return it directly. Otherwise it obtains the answer from the appropriate authoritative path and caches it according to the record's TTL.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Choose TTLs with change frequency and operational recovery in mind. Lower TTLs can make planned changes propagate sooner but increase lookup traffic. DNS should not be treated as an instantaneous failover mechanism unless the entire client and caching behavior has been considered.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: DNS is a distributed cache of answers. The key operational question is how long old answers can remain visible.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Explain authoritative servers, recursive resolution, TTL, and why DNS alone is not a magic instant failover mechanism.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid treating dns as a universal solution. State assumptions, identify the main bottleneck or failure mode, and explain the operational cost. Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
Use DNS for stable naming and coarse routing; pair it with health-aware traffic management when fast failover matters.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
DNS responses can remain cached at recursive resolvers and clients, so changes are not instantaneous.

topics.title: Load Balancing
topics.description: Learn how load balancers distribute traffic, detect unhealthy nodes, and influence application scalability.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Distribute traffic across healthy instances while considering capacity, connection behavior, and routing strategy.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A load balancer spreads requests across backend instances and can stop sending traffic to unhealthy nodes. Common routing strategies include round robin, least connections, and client-derived hashing. The strategy should match workload characteristics. Health checks should test meaningful service readiness rather than only whether a process is listening on a port.

Deeper reasoning:
Load balancing works best when backend instances have predictable health and similar capacity. When requests vary widely in cost, connection-aware or workload-aware routing can be more appropriate. Health checks should represent readiness to serve real traffic, not merely process liveness.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: An API runs on three identical instances. Round-robin routing distributes requests approximately A, B, C, A, B, C. If instance B fails its health check, the balancer removes it and routes new requests to A and C until B becomes healthy again.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Keep application nodes as stateless as practical. If session affinity is used, understand the failure and rebalancing implications. Load balancing does not remove database bottlenecks; it can increase database pressure if more application instances share the same backend.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: A load balancer changes where work runs, not the total work. A downstream bottleneck can remain unchanged or worsen.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss health checks, sticky sessions, draining, TLS termination, and what happens when all backends are unhealthy.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid treating load balancing as a universal solution. State assumptions, identify the main bottleneck or failure mode, and explain the operational cost. Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
Keep nodes stateless where practical and use connection draining during deployments.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
Round robin works well for similar stateless instances; least-connections or hashing can fit other workloads.

topics.title: API Gateway
topics.description: Understand the role of an API gateway at the edge of a distributed application.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Provide an edge policy and routing boundary for authentication, rate limits, routing, request IDs, and protocol concerns.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
An API gateway provides a controlled entry point between clients and internal services. It can perform routing, authentication, request validation, rate limiting, throttling, request identification, TLS termination, and observability. Centralizing common edge behavior prevents every backend service from independently implementing the same concerns, but the gateway itself must be horizontally scalable and carefully designed so it does not become a bottleneck.

Deeper reasoning:
An API gateway is an edge policy boundary, not a place to move every business rule. Centralize cross-cutting concerns that truly apply at the edge, while keeping domain decisions in the service that owns the business data.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A mobile application sends GET /courses/42. The gateway authenticates the request, checks the rate limit, attaches a request ID, and routes it to Course Service. A payment request can follow a different route and stricter policy without exposing internal service addresses to the client.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Keep business rules out of the gateway when they belong to domain services. Make gateway failures observable, avoid storing unnecessary session state there, and size gateway capacity for peak connection and request rates.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of the gateway as a traffic and policy boundary, not as the application's business brain.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Distinguish gateway responsibilities from domain business logic.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid treating api gateway as a universal solution. State assumptions, identify the main bottleneck or failure mode, and explain the operational cost. Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
Use it when multiple clients/services benefit from a controlled edge; avoid putting complex business workflows in it.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
The gateway centralizes cross-cutting edge behavior but can become a bottleneck or single operational dependency.

topics.title: CDN
topics.description: Learn how edge caching reduces latency and origin traffic for cacheable content.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Cache suitable content close to users to reduce origin load and latency.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A content delivery network stores cacheable objects at edge locations closer to users. A cache hit can be served without contacting the origin; a miss causes the edge to retrieve the object and may cache it for later requests. CDN effectiveness depends on cacheability, object popularity, freshness rules, and geographic distribution.

Deeper reasoning:
CDN performance depends heavily on cacheability. Public immutable assets are easier to cache than personalized responses. Cache keys, freshness rules, invalidation, and content versioning therefore matter as much as geographic edge placement.

A learner in Singapore can receive cached assets from a nearby edge rather than fetching every object from an origin region elsewhere. The application servers can therefore spend more capacity on dynamic requests.

sections.content: A CDN is a distributed read cache at the edge. Its value comes from high hit rate and safe cacheability.

topics.title: Caching
topics.description: Learn cache-aside, write-through behavior, TTL, invalidation, hit rate, and thundering-herd protection.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Reduce repeated backend work with explicit freshness, invalidation, eviction, and stampede controls.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Caching stores frequently used data closer to consumers so repeated work can be avoided. In cache-aside, the application reads the cache first and fills it after a miss. Write-through designs update the cache together with the backing store. TTLs limit how long entries remain usable. Cache design must explicitly address stale data, invalidation, eviction, hot keys, and concurrent misses.

Deeper reasoning:
Caching is an optimization layer, so the source of truth and stale-data policy must remain clear. A cache outage should normally degrade performance rather than destroy correctness. Treat cache misses as an expected path and protect the backing store from sudden miss storms.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A course catalog request checks course:42 in cache. On a miss, the application reads the database, stores the result with a short expiration, and returns it. A price update can invalidate the corresponding cache key so the next read obtains the new value.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Measure hit rate and backend load rather than assuming a cache is helping. A popular key that expires for thousands of clients at once can create a thundering herd. Jittered TTLs, request coalescing, early refresh, and controlled locking are possible mitigations.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The cache should be disposable. Correctness should remain understandable when every cache entry disappears.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss stale data, hot keys, cache stampedes, cache outages, and source-of-truth ownership.

topics.title: Database Selection

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Choose storage from access patterns, transaction semantics, consistency, scale, data shape, and operational constraints.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Database selection should begin with access patterns, consistency needs, transaction requirements, data shape, scale, growth, and operational constraints. Deeper reasoning:
Database choice becomes clearer when you write the most important queries first. If the common query is difficult or expensive in the proposed model, the model is probably not aligned with the workload. Schema design and database selection should therefore be driven by access patterns together.

topics.title: Replication
topics.description: Understand multiple data copies, synchronous versus asynchronous replication, lag, and durability trade-offs.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Maintain additional copies for availability, durability, or read scaling while handling lag and failover.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Replication maintains additional copies of data so reads, availability, or durability can be improved. Synchronous replication waits for specified replicas before acknowledging a write, while asynchronous replication acknowledges earlier and allows replicas to catch up later. Replication is not the same as backup: a replication stream can reproduce accidental or malicious changes, whereas backups provide historical recovery points.

Deeper reasoning:
Replication improves availability or read capacity only when the application understands replica behavior. Lag, failover, stale reads, and recovery all change the semantics of the system. Historical backups are a separate control because replicas can reproduce unwanted changes.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A primary database records a profile update and asynchronously sends the change to two replicas. A read routed immediately to a lagging replica might still see the previous value. If the product requires read-after-write behavior, recent reads can be routed to the primary or use a consistency-aware strategy.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Monitor replication lag and define what happens when a replica falls behind. Choose synchronous guarantees only where the added latency and availability implications are acceptable. Plan backups independently from replication.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Every replica adds another state that can be behind. Correctness depends on which copy a read observes.

sections.title: Interview focus

topics.title: Distributed Unique ID Generation

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Generate identifiers without a single overloaded allocator while considering uniqueness, ordering, size, locality, and privacy.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A single counter is easy to reason about, but multiple writers need a strategy that prevents collisions without creating unacceptable coordination. Central database sequences provide strong uniqueness but may become a shared dependency. UUID-style identifiers avoid central allocation in many designs at the cost of larger values and possible index-locality concerns. Time-structured IDs can combine time, node identity, and a sequence component.

Deeper reasoning:
An identifier is more than a unique number: it may influence ordering, indexing, privacy, and partitioning. A globally unique identifier that creates poor index locality or reveals sensitive timing may be technically correct but operationally undesirable.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A media service has ten upload workers creating asset records concurrently. Instead of asking one central service for every integer, each worker can generate a globally unique identifier using a scheme designed for distributed generation. The identifier can be stored as the durable asset key while a human-readable filename remains separate.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Evaluate uniqueness, ordering, size, privacy, generation cost, collision handling, and database indexing. Do not expose internal sequence information when it leaks sensitive business volume or ordering information.

sections.content: An ID is also an index key, ordering signal, and sometimes an information leak.

topics.title: Large File Uploads

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Move large payloads directly to object storage with scoped authorization, multipart/chunking, checksums, and resumability.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Large uploads should avoid unnecessarily routing the full payload through application servers. A common pattern is for the application to authenticate the user and issue temporary, narrowly scoped upload authorization for object storage. The client uploads chunks, retries failed chunks, and finalizes the object after all parts succeed. This reduces application-server bandwidth and makes interrupted transfers cheaper to resume.

Deeper reasoning:
Large-file architecture is mostly about moving bytes efficiently and recovering from partial failure. Authorization, upload state, checksums, chunk retries, and finalization should be designed as a state machine rather than as one giant request.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: For a 3 GB video, the client requests permission for an upload, receives short-lived authorization, and uploads multiple parts directly to storage. If part 12 fails, only that part is retried. Once all parts are present, the upload is finalized and metadata is recorded.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Balance chunk size against request overhead and retry cost. Limit parallel uploads so clients and storage are not overwhelmed. Validate file type, size, destination ownership, expiration, and checksums. Never expose broad permanent storage credentials.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Model upload as a state machine: initiated, parts uploaded, finalized, verified, processed, or expired.

topics.title: Object Storage

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Store large blobs in object storage while keeping transactional metadata in a database.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Object storage is designed for large immutable or versioned blobs such as images, videos, documents, and backups. A transactional database can keep ownership, status, object key, dimensions, and timestamps while the binary bytes live in object storage. Deeper reasoning:
Object storage works especially well when binary payloads can be addressed independently of transactional metadata. This separation also enables different lifecycle, access-control, CDN, and processing policies for the bytes.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Treat object keys as data identifiers rather than user-controlled filesystem paths. Control access with scoped authorization, validate metadata, consider lifecycle policies, and place frequently watched public assets behind a CDN.

sections.content: Metadata answers what the object means; object storage answers where its bytes live.

topics.title: Distributed Cache

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Partition cache entries across nodes while managing rebalancing, eviction, hot keys, and node failure.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A distributed cache spreads entries across multiple nodes so total memory and throughput exceed a single machine's practical capacity. A routing strategy maps keys to nodes. The design must account for eviction, expiration, node loss, rebalancing, and hot keys. A single extremely popular key can overload one node even when aggregate cache utilization looks healthy.

Deeper reasoning:
Distributed caching introduces cluster-level failure modes. Rebalancing, node loss, hot keys, and cache stampedes can turn a local optimization into a system-wide incident, so per-node telemetry is essential.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A catalog cache hashes product IDs across three cache nodes. Most products distribute evenly, but a homepage key becomes extremely popular. Rather than allowing every request to hammer one node, the system can use local caching, controlled replication, or request coalescing for that hot value.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Choose a partitioning strategy that minimizes unnecessary movement during scaling. Monitor per-node traffic and memory, not just cluster totals. Define what happens on a cache miss or node loss so the primary database is not suddenly overwhelmed.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Distribution solves aggregate capacity, not skew. Per-node telemetry is essential.

topics.title: Database Sharding

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Partition rows across nodes using a shard key chosen from real access patterns.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Sharding partitions a dataset across database nodes. Hash-based sharding can distribute records evenly, while range-based partitioning can make certain range queries natural. The shard key is critical because it determines where data and traffic land. A poor key can create hot shards, uneven storage, and expensive cross-shard operations.

Deeper reasoning:
Sharding changes the application because routing becomes part of data access. The shard key should support the most important queries, and the design should have a credible plan for growth, migration, and cross-shard operations.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A user service shards accounts using a stable user identifier. The application can route requests for a user directly to the responsible shard. If one customer organization generates a huge share of traffic and all its data lands together, the design may still produce a hot partition despite good average distribution.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Select keys from real access patterns, not only from data cardinality. Plan how resharding works, how secondary indexes behave, and how cross-shard transactions or queries are handled.

topics.title: Database Replicas and Read Scaling

sections.title: Concept

Applications therefore need a policy for read-after-write behavior, stale data tolerance, and replica selection.

Deeper reasoning:
Read replicas are useful only for reads that can tolerate their consistency model. A common pattern is to keep the primary on paths that require immediate visibility while sending eligible read-heavy traffic to replicas.

If the request goes to a replica that has not caught up, the response may contain the previous value. The application can route the user's recent reads to the primary or use a consistency-aware mechanism.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Monitor lag and remove unhealthy replicas from read rotation. Do not send every read to replicas merely because they exist; classify reads by freshness requirements.

sections.content: A replica is a different observation point of the same logical state; lag is a product-visible property when freshness matters.

topics.title: Consistency and Availability Trade-offs
topics.description: Learn how consistency requirements should be tied to business impact rather than treated as a single global setting.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Choose consistency per workflow based on the cost of stale or conflicting state.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Consistency describes what different readers can observe about shared state, while availability concerns whether the system continues responding during failures. Stronger consistency often requires more coordination, which can increase latency or reduce operation during some failures. Eventual consistency permits temporary divergence while allowing systems to scale and operate with looser coordination.

Deeper reasoning:
Consistency is best specified as a business requirement. Saying 'strong consistency everywhere' can create unnecessary coordination, while 'eventual consistency everywhere' can violate critical invariants. Classify each workflow by the harm caused by stale or conflicting state.

sections.content: A bank balance generally needs stronger correctness guarantees than a social-media like count. If a like counter is briefly behind, the user experience may still be acceptable; if a payment balance is stale during a withdrawal, the consequences are much more serious.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Classify data by business impact. For each workflow, define what stale data means, how long staleness is acceptable, and what operations require transactional guarantees. Consistency should be designed per operation or data domain when appropriate.

topics.title: Message Queues
topics.description: Understand producer-consumer decoupling, asynchronous work, backpressure, retries, and dead-letter handling.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Buffer asynchronous work between producers and consumers while defining delivery, retry, ordering, and idempotency semantics.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A message queue buffers work between producers and consumers. This allows a user-facing request to finish without waiting for every secondary task and lets workers process jobs at their own rate. Queues also absorb short traffic bursts, but they do not create infinite capacity: if production continuously exceeds consumption, backlog grows until capacity or retention limits are reached.

Deeper reasoning:
Queue-based designs shift some complexity from request latency into delivery semantics. Once work becomes asynchronous, the system must define what happens if a message is duplicated, delayed, reordered, or permanently rejected. These semantics are part of the application contract.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: When a user uploads a document, the API stores it and publishes a processing job. Workers consume jobs to extract text, create previews, and run validation. If processing temporarily slows, the queue holds pending work instead of forcing every upload request to wait.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Define retry limits, visibility or acknowledgement behavior, idempotency, ordering requirements, and dead-letter handling. Monitor queue depth and age, not just worker CPU. A growing backlog is a capacity signal, not merely a messaging metric.

sections.title: Deep mental model

topics.title: Communication Protocols

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Choose HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, WebSocket, or other mechanisms from interaction pattern, compatibility, streaming, and operational constraints.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Communication protocols determine how components exchange information. HTTP is a common request-response foundation, HTTPS adds TLS protection, gRPC provides strongly defined service contracts and efficient binary communication, and WebSocket provides persistent bidirectional messaging. Protocol choice should follow interaction patterns, compatibility needs, latency expectations, streaming requirements, and operational tooling rather than fashion.

Deeper reasoning:
Protocol selection should consider both wire behavior and operational reality. A theoretically efficient protocol can still be a poor choice if clients cannot support it, debugging is difficult, or the communication pattern does not match the protocol's strengths.

sections.content: A public browser API can use HTTPS with conventional HTTP methods. Internal services with stable typed contracts can use gRPC. sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Document timeout behavior, payload limits, versioning, and error semantics at every protocol boundary. A fast protocol does not compensate for poor data access or excessive network hops.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Protocol choice defines how failure, framing, retries, versioning, and observability behave at the boundary.

topics.title: WebSocket

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Maintain bidirectional connections for low-latency live interaction while handling connection ownership and reconnects.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
WebSocket provides a persistent two-way channel after the connection is established. This is useful when a server needs to push updates without waiting for another client request. At scale, the hard problems become connection count, memory per connection, heartbeats, reconnect storms, message routing, and knowing which server owns a user's live connection.

Deeper reasoning:
A live connection is ephemeral. Important application state should therefore be durable or reconstructable outside the socket. Connection registries tell the system where to deliver now, while message history or state snapshots make recovery possible later.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Persist important messages independently of the live connection. On reconnect, authenticate again, determine the last acknowledged event, replay missed state when required, and then resume live delivery.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: A socket is a transport session, not durable application state. Recovery needs an external source of truth.

topics.title: Short Polling
topics.description: Understand periodic request polling, its simplicity, and its cost at scale.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Repeatedly request state at fixed intervals when simplicity outweighs the request overhead.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Short polling repeatedly asks a server whether new information exists. It is easy to implement because it uses ordinary request-response infrastructure, but every interval produces a request even when nothing has changed. At high client counts, idle polling can consume significant network, connection, and server resources.

Deeper reasoning:
Polling trades implementation simplicity for repeated work. The right interval is a product decision as well as a technical one: shorter intervals improve freshness but increase load, while longer intervals save resources but make changes appear later.

sections.content: A small internal dashboard asks GET /job-status every five seconds. With only a few operators, the simplicity may be acceptable. If hundreds of thousands of clients use the same approach, most requests may return unchanged state and create unnecessary load.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Use short polling when update frequency and scale make the overhead acceptable. Increase the interval when freshness permits, add caching where appropriate, and move to event-driven delivery when idle traffic becomes a material cost.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Polling buys simplicity by paying repeated request cost. Scale determines whether that cost is acceptable.

topics.title: Long Polling

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Keep a request open until new data or a timeout, reducing empty responses without requiring a persistent bidirectional protocol.

sections.title: Detailed explanation

With long polling, the client sends a request and the server keeps it open until useful data arrives, a timeout occurs, or an error happens. The client then opens another request. This can reduce empty responses compared with short polling, but servers, proxies, and load balancers must handle many outstanding requests and clean timeout behavior.

Deeper reasoning:
Long polling reduces empty responses but still creates a large population of outstanding requests. Connection timeouts, proxy behavior, cancellation, and reconnect storms must therefore be designed explicitly.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Publish one business event to multiple independent consumers so secondary workloads scale and fail independently.

Fan-out reduces coupling by letting consumers evolve independently, but it also multiplies delivery paths. Each consumer needs its own retry, monitoring, and failure policy so one broken consumer does not stall unrelated work.

sections.content: Use durable event delivery for important side effects. Make consumers independently idempotent and observable. If a consumer is down, its backlog should be isolated rather than preventing unrelated consumers from progressing.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: One event can become many derived workflows; each consumer owns its own success and failure state.

Payments combine business state, external providers, and financial consequences. A request can time out after the provider has accepted it, so the client and server may not know the final outcome immediately. Idempotency keys prevent repeated requests from creating duplicate charges, while reconciliation resolves ambiguous states and mismatches between internal and provider records.

Deeper reasoning:
Financial workflows require explicit state because network uncertainty creates ambiguous outcomes. Treat 'unknown' as a real state that can be reconciled rather than guessing success or failure after a timeout.

If the client retries because the network failed, the service returns the existing result instead of starting another independent charge. A background reconciliation process can compare internal records with provider records.

topics.title: Distributed Locking
topics.description: Understand distributed coordination, lock ownership, leases, expiration, and when a lock is actually appropriate.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Coordinate competing workers with ownership, leases, expiration, and careful failure semantics.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A distributed lock coordinates competing workers when duplicate execution would be harmful or wasteful. A robust lock needs ownership so one worker cannot accidentally release another worker's lock, an expiration or lease so a crashed owner does not hold it forever, and careful handling of renewal and network uncertainty. Locks should solve a specific correctness or coordination problem rather than being added automatically.

Deeper reasoning:
Distributed locks can prevent duplicate concurrent work, but they cannot magically make a multi-step operation atomic. If correctness can be achieved with database constraints or idempotent operations, those mechanisms may be easier to reason about than a lock.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Two workers receive requests to generate the same expensive report. A lock keyed by report ID lets one worker become the active generator while the other waits or observes that work is already in progress. The lock expires if the owner disappears unexpectedly.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Use atomic acquisition with an owner token where supported. Keep the protected critical section bounded and consider what happens if the lock expires while work is still running. If duplicate work is acceptable, idempotent processing may be safer and simpler than distributed locking.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: A distributed lock is a coordination hint with failure modes; correctness must not depend on an impossible guarantee.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss owner tokens, lease expiry, renewal, fencing where relevant, and alternatives such as database constraints or idempotency.

topics.title: Observability

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Observability provides evidence about what a system is doing internally. Logs capture structured events, metrics show aggregate behavior over time, and distributed traces connect work across service boundaries. Request IDs and trace IDs make it possible to correlate a user action with downstream calls. Good observability measures both health and user-visible behavior.

Deeper reasoning:
Observability should connect symptoms to causes. A high error rate without request context is less useful than a trace that identifies the slow dependency and logs that carry the same correlation identifiers.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A checkout request has trace ID t-812. The trace shows 25 ms in the gateway, 40 ms in the order service, 280 ms waiting on inventory, and 35 ms in payment preparation. The same trace ID appears in structured logs, allowing an operator to move from a latency symptom to the responsible dependency.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Measure request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, queue depth, cache hit rate, database latency, saturation, and replication lag where relevant. Avoid logging secrets or unnecessary personal data. Alerts should indicate actionable conditions rather than every transient fluctuation.

topics.title: Advanced Reliability Patterns
topics.description: Learn circuit breakers, bulkheads, graceful degradation, bounded retries, and failure isolation as complementary reliability techniques.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Combine timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, graceful degradation, bounded retries, and load shedding.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Advanced resilience patterns prevent one failing dependency from consuming all resources or turning a local fault into a system-wide outage. A circuit breaker can fail fast when a dependency is repeatedly unhealthy. Bulkheads isolate thread pools, connection pools, or queues by workload. Graceful degradation serves a reduced feature set. Bounded retries avoid infinite amplification.

Deeper reasoning:
Reliability patterns work best in combination. Timeouts bound waiting, circuit breakers stop repeated calls, bulkheads isolate resources, and graceful degradation defines a useful fallback. None of these should replace clear ownership and correct state transitions.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A marketplace uses separate resource pools for payment and recommendation calls. If recommendation becomes slow, its pool saturates without consuming every payment worker. A circuit breaker then stops new recommendation calls for a recovery period, while the product falls back to a generic ranking.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Tune thresholds from measured behavior rather than arbitrary numbers. Combine timeouts with circuit breakers and bulkheads. Ensure fallback behavior is safe and does not silently violate business correctness.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Reliability is resource containment plus recovery. Prevent one failure from consuming everything needed by healthy work.

topics.title: Idempotency in Depth
topics.description: Learn how repeated requests arise in distributed systems and how idempotency prevents duplicate effects.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Make repeated requests produce one intended business effect through stable request identities and durable result handling.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A request can be repeated because of client retries, timeouts, proxies, worker retries, or uncertain network outcomes. An idempotent operation produces the same intended business result when the same request is processed again. A practical design uses a stable request key, stores the resulting state, and returns the existing result when the key is seen again.

Deeper reasoning:
Idempotency is especially important when the caller cannot distinguish 'request failed' from 'response lost'. A stable key lets the server turn uncertain retries into a deterministic result.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A checkout client sends clientRequestId ABC123. The server creates order 900 and records ABC123 with that result. If the first response is lost and the client sends ABC123 again, the server recognizes the prior request and returns order 900 instead of creating another order.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Choose the idempotency key scope and retention period carefully. Store enough information to reproduce the prior response safely. Idempotency does not mean every internal step is magically safe; downstream calls may need their own deduplication or transactional strategy.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Idempotency converts an uncertain retry into a deterministic lookup of an existing outcome.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss key scope, retention, concurrent requests, response replay, and downstream idempotency.

topics.title: Data Consistency in Asynchronous Systems
topics.description: Learn why independent consumers can observe different states temporarily and how to design acceptable consistency windows.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Define acceptable freshness windows when consumers update independently.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Asynchronous architectures intentionally allow components to progress at different speeds. After a business event is emitted, one consumer may finish immediately while another is delayed. This is acceptable when the product defines a consistency window and users can tolerate it. When a requirement demands immediate visibility, that path needs stronger synchronization or a different read strategy.

Deeper reasoning:
Asynchronous consistency should be measured as lag, not treated as an abstract idea. Event age and consumer backlog reveal whether the system is within the product's accepted freshness window.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: After an order is created, analytics may already contain the event while the search index still shows the old catalog state and notification remains queued. These differences are not necessarily failures; they become failures only when they violate an explicit business requirement.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Define freshness targets per consumer. Monitor event lag and processing age. Provide repair or replay mechanisms so a failed consumer can catch up without requiring the originating transaction to be repeated.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Measure consistency as observable lag and define what lag is acceptable for each consumer.

sections.title: Interview focus

topics.title: Backpressure and Queue Sizing
topics.description: Learn how producer-consumer imbalance creates backlog and how simple capacity arithmetic guides scaling decisions.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Control producer-consumer imbalance using capacity math, admission control, prioritization, and scaling.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Backpressure appears when producers generate work faster than consumers can process it. If producers create 8,000 jobs per second and consumers complete 5,000, the backlog grows by about 3,000 jobs per second. A finite queue can therefore be exhausted after a calculable interval. Queue depth alone is less informative than queue growth rate and age of the oldest work.

Deeper reasoning:
Backpressure is a conservation problem: if arrival rate stays above service rate, backlog must grow. Capacity calculations make that fact visible and provide a basis for deciding when to scale or shed work.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: If a queue can hold 9 million jobs and backlog grows steadily by 3,000 jobs per second, capacity would be exhausted in about 3,000 seconds, or 50 minutes, under those assumptions. Adding workers, improving processing efficiency, reducing incoming work, or prioritizing jobs can change the outcome.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Monitor arrival rate, completion rate, depth, oldest-message age, retry volume, and worker saturation. Define overload behavior for low-priority work rather than allowing every workload to compete equally.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Backpressure is a feedback mechanism: when downstream capacity falls, upstream work must slow, buffer, or be rejected.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss queue depth, oldest-item age, arrival/service rates, worker concurrency, and overload behavior.

topics.title: Hot Partitions
topics.description: Learn why average distribution can look healthy while a small number of keys or entities overload individual partitions.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Detect skew where a small set of keys overload one partition despite balanced average distribution.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Partitioning distributes data by a routing key, but workload distribution is not always the same as data distribution. A celebrity account, popular product, or heavily accessed tenant can create a hot partition even when the shard function is mathematically balanced. Hotspots require workload-aware mitigation.

Deeper reasoning:
Hotspots require workload-aware partitioning. A perfectly balanced hash can still fail if one entity receives a disproportionate fraction of traffic. Protecting hot entities may require replication or a different access path.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A user database hashes user IDs across 16 partitions. Most users generate little traffic, but one public account receives a huge share of reads. All of that account's requests still target one partition, which becomes CPU-bound while the other partitions remain lightly loaded.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Use caching, replicated hot values, request coalescing, workload splitting, or specialized routing when appropriate. Monitor per-partition traffic and latency rather than relying only on cluster-wide averages.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Average load hides tail concentration. Always inspect the busiest partition, not just the cluster average.

sections.content: Discuss hot tenants, celebrity keys, salting, replication, local caching, and per-partition telemetry.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Separate functional requirements, quality attributes, assumptions, scope, and explicit constraints.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Requirement gathering defines the problem before architecture is selected. Functional requirements describe behavior; non-functional requirements describe qualities such as latency, availability, durability, security, and scale. Assumptions should be written down because architecture decisions depend on them. Clear requirements prevent overbuilding and expose the trade-offs that actually matter.

Deeper reasoning:
Requirements are assumptions that can be measured and challenged. Explicitly separating must-have features from optional behavior prevents architecture from being shaped by features that may never be used.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: For a food-delivery platform, functional requirements might include restaurant browsing, ordering, driver assignment, and delivery tracking. sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Separate must-have behavior from optional features. Record expected traffic, peak multipliers, object sizes, geographic scope, retention, and consistency needs. Revisit assumptions when workload measurements change.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: A design is an answer to a constraint set. Change the constraints and a different architecture may become correct.

topics.title: Capacity Estimation
topics.description: Learn to estimate request rate, peak load, storage growth, and bandwidth before committing to architecture.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Estimate requests, concurrency, storage, bandwidth, and peak factors before selecting infrastructure.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Capacity estimation converts vague scale statements into approximate numbers. For example, 2 million daily users making 20 requests each produce 40 million requests per day, or roughly 463 requests per second on average. A peak multiplier can then estimate burst traffic. Similar arithmetic can estimate storage and network volume. These numbers are planning tools, not promises of exact production behavior.

Deeper reasoning:
Estimation does not need perfect numbers to be useful. Even rough arithmetic can reveal whether a single node, database, network link, or queue could plausibly handle the expected workload.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: If an application receives 50 million requests per day, the average rate is about 579 requests per second. If a design must handle an assumed 8x peak, the planning target becomes roughly 4,630 requests per second. If each response averages 12 KB, the payload bandwidth can then be estimated from the peak request rate.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Use generous but explicit assumptions and label them. Estimate storage with indexes, replicas, backups, and growth included. Capacity planning should be revisited after real telemetry is available.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Capacity planning is about bounding the problem so component limits can be compared with expected demand.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Reuse patterns such as cache-aside, async processing, replication, sharding, fan-out, circuit breakers, and bulkheads when their assumptions fit.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
System design patterns are reusable responses to recurring problems. Cache-aside reduces repeated backend work, queues decouple slow tasks, fan-out separates consumers, replication provides copies, sharding partitions data, circuit breakers stop repeated calls to failing dependencies, and bulkheads isolate resource pools. Patterns are tools, not mandatory components.

Deeper reasoning:
Patterns are reusable only when their assumptions are understood. For example, cache-aside assumes a source of truth remains available, while sharding assumes requests can be routed using the chosen partition key. Learning the assumptions is more valuable than memorizing the pattern name.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A marketplace uses cache-aside for popular product details, a queue for invoice generation, a fan-out event for analytics and notifications, and a circuit breaker around a recommendation provider. Each pattern exists because of a concrete workload or failure characteristic.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Always state the problem a pattern solves and the cost it introduces. A queue adds eventual processing and operational complexity; sharding adds routing and cross-partition challenges; a circuit breaker requires sensible thresholds and recovery behavior.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Every pattern has a trigger condition and a downside. Memorizing names without those is weak system-design reasoning.

topics.title: Iterative Design
topics.description: Learn how to evolve a system from a simple architecture as measured workload and requirements grow.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Start with a simple viable architecture, identify bottlenecks and risks, then evolve the design as scale and requirements demand.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A good architecture evolves in stages. A small product may start with a client, application server, and database. As traffic grows, a load balancer can distribute application instances; caching can reduce repeated reads; queues can move expensive work off the request path; replicas or sharding can address database constraints. The sequence should follow observed bottlenecks rather than speculation.

Deeper reasoning:
Iterative architecture reduces premature complexity. A simple version can provide real measurements that guide the next change, making later distribution decisions evidence-based instead of speculative.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Version one of a study portal uses one application and one database. When read traffic grows, a cache is introduced. When document processing becomes slow, jobs move to workers through a queue. When read capacity becomes the next bottleneck, replicas are evaluated.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Keep the architecture understandable at each stage. Introduce a component only when it solves a known problem or provides a justified operational capability. Record why a component exists so future engineers can remove it when it is no longer useful.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: A good architecture is not static. It is a sequence of safer states with migration paths between them.

topics.title: Testing and Validation
topics.description: Learn how to validate functionality, load behavior, failure handling, and recovery.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Validate architecture with functional, load, failure, consistency, security, and recovery tests.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Distributed systems need more than unit tests. Functional tests verify correctness; load tests expose capacity and latency behavior; failure tests reveal how the system behaves when dependencies disappear; recovery tests verify that service can return after faults. A backup that has never been restored is an assumption, not a proven recovery mechanism.

Deeper reasoning:
Validation should test both correctness and behavior under stress. A system that works at low load can still fail because of connection exhaustion, queue growth, replication lag, or retry amplification.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A service is tested at expected peak traffic while measuring p95 latency and error rate. A database replica is then made unavailable, a queue backlog is introduced, and a dependency timeout is simulated. Finally, a restore procedure is exercised in an isolated environment and the recovered data is validated.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Test realistic failure modes and define pass/fail criteria. Include degraded dependencies, delayed messages, duplicate events, network errors, and restart scenarios. Validate recovery time and data loss objectives where those requirements exist.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Validation turns architectural assumptions into evidence. A diagram is a hypothesis until tested.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss load tests, chaos/failure injection, contract tests, replay, recovery drills, and data-integrity checks.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid treating testing and validation as a universal solution. State assumptions, identify the main bottleneck or failure mode, and explain the operational cost. Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
Test the highest-risk assumptions first rather than only happy paths.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
Distributed correctness cannot be established by unit tests alone.

In production, pair the design with monitoring, capacity limits, safe rollout and a recovery procedure. Define what operators should observe when the component is degraded.
