topics.title: Documentation
topics.description: Learn what an architecture document should record and why trade-offs must be explicit.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Document requirements, architecture, data ownership, APIs, failure behavior, decisions, and operational procedures.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Architecture documentation captures requirements, assumptions, APIs, data ownership, scaling expectations, failure modes, security decisions, consistency choices, and trade-offs. Good documentation explains not only what was selected but why alternatives were rejected. This preserves decision context and reduces repeated design work.

Deeper reasoning:
Documentation is part of system reliability because future operators need to know why a dependency exists and what assumptions it relies on. Record decisions in terms that can be checked against production measurements.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A media platform documents that direct-to-object-storage uploads were chosen because application servers should not carry multi-gigabyte payloads. It also records the trade-off: upload authorization and completion tracking become more complex, and the platform must monitor incomplete uploads.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Keep diagrams and written contracts synchronized with implementation. Record assumptions that can expire, such as traffic forecasts or retention periods. Documentation should help an engineer operate and change the system, not merely describe boxes.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Documentation is an externalized architectural memory that reduces repeated rediscovery.

sections.title: Interview focus

topics.title: Common Design Mistakes
topics.description: Learn recurring architectural mistakes involving premature technology choices, missing numbers, failure handling, hotspots, and incorrect use of synchronous or asynchronous work.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Avoid premature microservices, technology-first design, unbounded retries, single bottlenecks, unclear ownership, and missing failure plans.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Common mistakes usually come from skipping reasoning steps. Choosing technologies before defining the workload can create unnecessary complexity. Ignoring numbers hides capacity problems. Ignoring failures produces fragile designs. Synchronous-everything increases coupling, while asynchronous-everything can make critical state transitions confusing. Lack of idempotency and observability makes retries and diagnosis much harder.

Deeper reasoning:
Design mistakes are often symptoms of missing reasoning rather than missing technology. A useful review asks whether every component has a workload, failure, and operational justification.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Instead of starting with a list of products, begin with requirements, workload, constraints, architecture, and then technology choices. If a service is expected to handle 10 million users, estimate request rate, peak traffic, storage, and bandwidth before deciding whether sharding or a queue is necessary.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Review every component by asking what problem it solves, what happens when it fails, and how it scales. Look specifically for hot keys, hot partitions, unbounded retries, unbounded queues, and hidden synchronous dependencies.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The most dangerous architecture is often the one that has no defined behavior when something goes wrong.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interviewers value recognizing trade-offs and failure modes more than naming many technologies.

sections.title: Common pitfalls

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
Many weak designs work on the happy path but have no answer for overload, duplicate delivery, partial failure, or recovery.

topics.title: System Design Review Checklist
topics.description: Learn a reusable checklist for reviewing functionality, scale, performance, reliability, data, asynchronous processing, real-time behavior, media, security, and observability.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Review requirements, traffic, APIs, storage, scaling, consistency, resilience, security, observability, cost, and operations.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A design review should examine the system from several angles. Functionality covers features, APIs, data models, and flows. Scale covers users, request rates, peaks, storage, and bandwidth. Reliability covers replication, failover, retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, recovery, and degradation. Data review covers indexes, partitioning, read/write patterns, and consistency. Async, real-time, media, security, and observability each need their own checks.

Deeper reasoning:
A checklist is valuable because distributed designs have many dimensions that are easy to forget. It should be the final verification layer after the architecture and trade-offs have already been reasoned through.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Before launching a document platform, review whether uploads are authorized and resumable, whether processing jobs have retry and dead-letter behavior, whether search indexing can recover, whether CDN caching is safe, whether database backups have been restored successfully, and whether traces can identify slow requests.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Use the checklist as a final pass, not as a substitute for design reasoning. Every checked item should have a concrete implementation or documented decision behind it.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Review the design as a lifecycle: build, deploy, serve, fail, recover, migrate, and retire.

sections.title: Interview focus

topics.title: Complete Example: Video Platform
topics.description: Study a complete video-platform architecture that combines storage, asynchronous processing, search, recommendations, and edge delivery.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Design upload, metadata, transcoding, storage, playback, CDN delivery, search, and asynchronous processing as separate concerns.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A video platform has two very different paths: metadata and control operations are relatively small, while video bytes and processing workloads are large. A scalable design separates these concerns. The client reaches the application through an edge layer; metadata services manage ownership and state; uploads use temporary authorization to object storage; processing workers transcode and generate thumbnails; CDN infrastructure serves popular processed media.

Deeper reasoning:
The video example demonstrates why data size changes architecture. Large media, transactional metadata, asynchronous processing, and global delivery have different resource profiles and should not be forced through one synchronous path.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A creator requests an upload authorization, uploads a 1.2 GB video directly to object storage, and marks the upload complete. A queue triggers transcoding and moderation workers. Once processed objects are ready, metadata is updated and the CDN can serve playback assets. Search indexing and recommendation updates happen asynchronously.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Keep large bytes off the synchronous API path. Track processing states such as uploading, processing, ready, and failed. Design for partial upload retries, worker retries, object lifecycle cleanup, and CDN cache behavior.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Video systems are byte-heavy and compute-heavy. Separate control-plane metadata from data-plane media delivery.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss multipart upload, transcoding queues, multiple renditions, CDN caching, access control, and processing retries.

sections.content: Avoid treating complete example: video platform as a universal solution. State assumptions, identify the main bottleneck or failure mode, and explain the operational cost. Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

sections.content:
Use asynchronous workflows because encoding can take much longer than an interactive API request.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

topics.title: Complete Example: Chat System
topics.description: Study the architecture of a scalable chat system including live connections, message persistence, routing, and reconnect recovery.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Design persistent conversations, message writes, delivery, presence, reconnects, history, and fan-out.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Chat combines persistent connections with durable message state. WebSocket servers manage live connections, while a connection registry helps locate where a user is connected. Messages should have durable identifiers and persistence semantics independent of the live socket. Queues or messaging infrastructure can decouple routing and processing. Reconnect logic must recover missed messages rather than assuming connections are permanent.

Deeper reasoning:
Chat systems illustrate the difference between connection state and message state. A socket can disappear at any time, so durable message identity and recovery rules are essential for reliable user experience.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A sender creates message 8001 for conversation 44. The message service persists it and determines that the recipient is connected to WebSocket node B. Node B delivers it live. If the recipient disconnects, the next connection authenticates, identifies the last acknowledged message, requests missed messages, and then returns to live delivery.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Plan for reconnect storms, duplicate delivery, ordering requirements, offline users, message retention, and connection-server failure. The live channel should be treated as a delivery mechanism, not the only copy of important state.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Chat is two systems joined together: durable conversation state and ephemeral connection state.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss WebSocket connection routing, message IDs, ordering scope, offline delivery, and reconnect behavior.

topics.title: Complete Example: E-Commerce Platform
topics.description: Study how catalog, cart, order, payment, search, recommendation, cache, queues, and notifications fit into one business architecture.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Design catalog, search, cart, inventory, order, payment, and notification flows with clear ownership.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
An e-commerce platform contains transactional and secondary workloads with different correctness needs. Catalog and order data need durable transactional handling, while analytics, recommendations, and many notifications can be asynchronous. The architecture therefore combines an edge layer, gateway, domain services, cache, primary data store, queues, object storage, and independent consumers.

Deeper reasoning:
E-commerce combines strict and relaxed consistency in one product. Order and payment state need strong protection, while analytics and recommendations can often tolerate delayed processing. Architecture should reflect those different business priorities.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A customer submits an order. The order service validates inventory, creates the order, coordinates payment, and publishes an OrderCreated event. Notification and analytics consumers process the event independently. If notification is unavailable, the completed order does not need to be rolled back merely because a secondary side effect is delayed.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Keep the critical transaction narrow. Use idempotency for retried order or payment requests, define inventory consistency carefully, and make secondary consumers independently retryable and observable.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: E-commerce design is primarily about preserving business invariants while many independent components fail or retry.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss inventory races, idempotent order creation, payment uncertainty, search lag, caching, and order events.

topics.title: Deep Example: URL Shortener
topics.description: Study a complete URL-shortening design with identifier generation, caching, read-heavy traffic, and failure considerations.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Map short codes to destination URLs with fast reads, unique code generation, abuse controls, and analytics.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A URL shortener maps a compact code to an original URL and redirects users when the code is requested. Creation traffic is usually much smaller than redirect traffic, so the architecture should optimize the read path. A durable mapping store provides the source of truth, while popular codes can be cached near the application or edge.

Deeper reasoning:
A URL shortener is a useful example of asymmetric traffic: creation is relatively small while redirects can be enormous. This naturally leads to a read-optimized architecture with aggressive caching and simple durable mappings.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A creation request stores a generated identifier mapped to https://example.test/articles/large-topic and returns a short code such as xY7k. A redirect request first checks a distributed cache for xY7k. On a miss it reads the mapping store, fills the cache, and redirects the client.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Use a collision-safe identifier strategy. Consider expiration, abuse controls, custom aliases, cache invalidation, analytics, and regional traffic. Because redirects can dominate traffic, edge caching and read scaling may matter more than optimizing creation.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The short code is both a routing key and a public identifier; its generation and privacy properties matter.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss ID generation, collision handling, redirects, hot links, expiration, rate limiting, and analytics fan-out.

topics.title: Deep Example: Notification Platform
topics.description: Study how a high-volume notification platform can separate event ingestion, preference checks, scheduling, and provider delivery.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Accept notification requests, apply preferences, schedule or fan out messages, deliver through providers, and track outcomes.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A notification platform receives business events and turns them into messages across channels. The architecture should separate ingestion from delivery so a slow provider does not block event producers. A queue buffers work, preference and template services determine what should be sent, and channel workers communicate with external providers. Delivery results can feed retry and analytics flows.

Deeper reasoning:
A notification platform demonstrates why provider calls should be decoupled from event ingestion. The system can absorb bursts, apply preferences, retry transient failures, and isolate provider-specific limits from the rest of the application.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: An order-completed event enters the notification pipeline. The system checks whether the user allows email, renders a receipt template, places the job on an email queue, and a worker calls the provider. A transient provider failure schedules bounded retry with backoff; a permanently failing message moves to a review path.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Partition work by channel or priority when necessary. Protect providers with rate limits, deduplicate repeated events, and track delivery states. Avoid sending notifications that violate user preferences even if an upstream event is duplicated.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Notification systems are workflow engines around unreliable external side effects.

sections.title: Interview focus

topics.title: Deep Example: Live Dashboard
topics.description: Study how a live operational dashboard can combine event streams, caching, WebSocket or SSE delivery, and resilient aggregation.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Combine streaming updates, aggregation, connection management, and historical snapshots for dashboards.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A live dashboard needs fresh data without forcing every browser to poll aggressively. An ingestion pipeline receives events, aggregation workers compute useful summaries, and a real-time delivery layer pushes updates to connected clients. A snapshot or cache can provide initial state before live events begin.

Deeper reasoning:
A live dashboard demonstrates a snapshot-plus-stream model. A snapshot gives a consistent starting point, while live events keep the view fresh. This also makes reconnect behavior easier to reason about.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A fleet dashboard receives vehicle telemetry through an ingestion stream. Aggregators maintain current counts and recent values. When a browser connects, it receives a current snapshot and then subscribes to live updates through SSE. If the connection drops, the client reconnects and receives a fresh snapshot before continuing.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: Define acceptable staleness and event ordering. Avoid sending every raw event to every browser if clients only need aggregates. Monitor connection counts, event rates, processing lag, and reconnect volume.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: A live dashboard is a read model that must answer both 'what is true now?' and 'what changed since I disconnected?'

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Discuss snapshot-plus-delta recovery, SSE/WebSocket choice, aggregation windows, backpressure, and reconnects.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid treating deep example: live dashboard as a universal solution. State assumptions, identify the main bottleneck or failure mode, and explain the operational cost. Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

Use a current-state snapshot plus incremental events when consumers need reliable recovery.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

topics.title: Practical Exercises
topics.description: Practice system-design reasoning through progressively richer architecture exercises without relying on memorized solutions.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Practice requirement gathering, capacity estimates, API design, data modeling, failure analysis, and trade-off explanation.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Practical exercises turn individual concepts into design judgment. Start with a small service and add constraints one at a time: more users, higher read traffic, larger objects, stricter consistency, regional failures, or bursty asynchronous work. The goal is to observe which component becomes the bottleneck and then introduce the smallest useful change.

Deeper reasoning:
Exercises are most useful when constraints change between iterations. Add traffic, failures, larger objects, stricter consistency, or new regions and observe which original assumptions break.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Exercise one: design a course catalog for 100,000 users. Exercise two: add 10 million daily reads and decide where caching belongs. Exercise three: add video uploads and move binary data to object storage. Exercise four: add live progress updates and compare polling, SSE, and WebSocket. Exercise five: simulate a database outage and document the degraded behavior.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: For each exercise, record requirements, estimates, APIs, data model, architecture, bottlenecks, failure modes, and trade-offs. After finishing, change one assumption and redesign only the affected portion.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Practice is strongest when every component has a reason, a failure mode, and a measurable trigger for scaling.

sections.title: Interview focus

topics.title: Master System Design Mental Model
topics.description: Build a reusable mental model that connects requirements, estimates, APIs, data, architecture, bottlenecks, reliability, security, and trade-offs.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Use a repeatable sequence: requirements, estimates, APIs, data model, high-level architecture, bottlenecks, reliability, security, observability, and trade-offs.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A compact mental model is: requirements -> workload -> constraints -> interfaces -> data model -> simple architecture -> bottleneck analysis -> scaling -> failure handling -> security -> observability -> trade-offs. The sequence keeps each decision connected to a reason. It also helps distinguish a necessary component from decorative complexity.

Deeper reasoning:
The mental model is a debugging tool as much as a design tool. When an architecture feels confusing, return to requirements and trace one critical request until every component has a reason.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Imagine a photo-sharing service. Requirements define upload, viewing, and sharing. Workload estimates show that reads dominate writes and photos are large. That leads toward CDN and object storage for media, a database for metadata, caching for popular objects, queues for image processing, and a real-time or notification path only where the product actually needs it.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: When stuck, return to the flow and ask one question at a time: what is the critical user path, what data does it need, what is slowest, what happens when it fails, and how will the system behave at peak load? This prevents premature jumping to infrastructure products.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think in four layers: user intent, system state, work flows, and failure/recovery flows.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interviewers often reward structured thinking, explicit assumptions, and awareness of failure modes.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Avoid treating master system design mental model as a universal solution. State assumptions, identify the main bottleneck or failure mode, and explain the operational cost. Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content:
Use the same mental sequence for unfamiliar products and adjust only the domain-specific details.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content:
The goal is not to memorize diagrams but to derive architecture from constraints.

In production, pair the design with monitoring, capacity limits, safe rollout and a recovery procedure. Define what operators should observe when the component is degraded.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Strong system design is disciplined trade-off analysis under scale, failure, consistency, security, and cost constraints.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Strong system design is disciplined trade-off management. Start with user behavior and measurable requirements. Choose data models from access patterns. Scale only the constrained component. Keep large or slow work off critical paths when appropriate. Treat failure, security, and observability as first-class design concerns. Prefer simple architectures until real requirements justify additional distribution.

Deeper reasoning:
The final synthesis is that scalable architecture is not a collection of products. It is a set of deliberate boundaries, data flows, capacity assumptions, failure behaviors, and trade-offs that fit the workload.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A mature architecture for a learning platform may combine a CDN for static assets, a load balancer for stateless application instances, a cache for hot reads, a transactional database for core state, object storage for files, queues for background work, specialized indexes for search, and observability across every boundary. Each component has a reason and a defined failure behavior.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.content: The best designs are explainable. An engineer should be able to trace a request through the system, identify where data lives, estimate capacity, describe what happens during failure, and explain why each major architectural choice was made.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The final test is whether you can explain why the system works, how it fails, and how you would know when it needs to change.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Summarize the chosen architecture, its assumptions, biggest bottleneck, most important failure mode, and next scaling step.

Do not hide important semantics such as consistency, ordering, retries, durability, or authorization behind a vague abstraction.

sections.title: When to use / avoid

Prefer simple architectures that can evolve safely over elaborate designs that have no operational justification.

Avoid it when the added complexity does not address a demonstrated requirement or when a simpler design provides the same guarantees.

A mature answer explains both the happy path and what happens when dependencies slow down, duplicate work, lose data, or fail.

In production, pair the design with monitoring, capacity limits, safe rollout and a recovery procedure. Define what operators should observe when the component is degraded.
